utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Will the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we please have the appearances, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution Daryl Mundis and Aditya Menon, assisted by our case manager Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis. From the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning to my learned friends from the Office of the Prosecution, to everyone in the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas David Robson on behalf of General Rasim Delic, with our assistant Ramovic and Vajvid Imamomic [as interpreted] from the Criminal Court of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Upon the motion of the Prosecution to which the Defence has agreed, the Trial Chamber sits today pursuant to Rule 4 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia, and sits in Sarajevo, Bosnia-Herzegovina. The purpose is to hear the evidence of a witness, and the Trial Chamber shall sit here pursuant to that Rule until the evidence is complete, and it is anticipated to finish by no later than the 9th of September, 2007. The situation in this court is slightly different from the situation in the court in The Hague in that we are not in a position to shut the gallery out, the public out, if we have to go into private session or closed session. When that has to happen, it is required that we clear the gallery. I'll therefore ask the parties to the extent possible to try to pen in or to deal with private matters or matters that require private session or closed session either at the beginning or at the end of the of the session so that there is minimum interruption with the public gallery. Thank you so much. May the witness please be called in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, you may be seated. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you please state your full name for the record, spelling your last name.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: My name is Ali Ahmad Ali Hamad. A-l-i; then Ahmad, A-h-m-a-d; then Ali, A-l-i; and then Hamad, H-a-m-a-d.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, can you please tell the Trial Chamber your place of birth and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I was born on the 11th -- no, the 13th of November, 1971, in Bahrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, did there come a time in your late teens when you left Bahrain?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes. I first travelled in the Arab world and then to Afghanistan when I joined in the war with the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, sir, approximately what year you travelled to Afghanistan and approximately how old you were at the time.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly when I travelled to Afghanistan, but I think it was at the beginning of 1991, and I think I was about 20 or 21 at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, how long did you remain in Afghanistan?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: About 13 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, that 13-month period, was it one continuous period or was it a period that was broken into smaller segments of time?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: This happened in several segments. The first trip was for three months. Then I went for a period of one month, and then for nine months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were you doing in Afghanistan, Mr. Hamad?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I joined the Mujahedin, that is, people who were under the command of Osama bin Laden and the organisation that is known today as al-Qaeda. So I was a combatant under the command of al-Qaeda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, during this -- this period of time totaling 13 months in Afghanistan, did you receive any type of military training?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes. During the first three months that I spent in Afghanistan I was in a training camp, and then during my second trip to Afghanistan I was also in a training camp for a month, and after that I attended a military academy organised personally by Osama bin Laden.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, did you tell us -- or tell the Trial Chamber about the specific type of military training that you received?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: The military academy I attended resembles very much a regular military academy. It is very capable and can equip an individual to use all the weapons in the possession of the Mujahedin in Afghanistan. A graduate of that academy should be able to use all kind of weapons manufactured in Russia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, you've mentioned Osama bin Laden on two occasions. Did you ever meet Mr. bin Laden while you were in Afghanistan?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: When I went to Afghanistan for the third time I met him on numerous occasions because, after all, I was a fighter in his organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where did you go, sir, after leaving Afghanistan for the third time? After the nine-month period where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: When my term in Afghanistan ended, I was told to go back to Bahrain, and there the same people ordered me to go to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you some questions to clarify that last answer. Who told you to return to Bahrain?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: We were told by Osama bin Laden and his commanders. I personally was told by Osama bin Laden.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what, if anything, do you recall Mr. bin Laden telling you to do after you returned to Bahrain?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: It was not the practice of al-Qaeda to tell us young soldiers what we should do when we left Afghanistan. We were simply told to go back from where we had come. And there were quite a number of us young combatants, and we were told that we would be told in our own countries where to go next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hamad, did you in fact receive subsequent instructions as to where to go next?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you please explain the word "instruksija" [phoen], "instructions", for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you receive, sir, an order to go somewhere or a direction to go somewhere, or were you told to go somewhere?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes. We were ordered to go from our own countries to go to wage war somewhere, and we thought we would be sent is to Kuwait to assist in liberating Kuwait from Saddam and his army. In the meantime, we learnt that once we returned to our countries we were told to go to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, do you recall approximately when you were told to go to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: This was at the beginning of the war. I heard about the war in Bosnia and all the events there at the beginning of 1992, and then I was told by people working for our al-Qaeda in Bahrain that I need to travel to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Hamad, the name or names of the people from al-Qaeda who directed you or ordered you to go to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: One of the al-Qaeda members was the prince of Bahrain, and I received my first orders from him. He intimated that this order did not come from him personally but an al-Qaeda cell. The other order came from Abdul Araf [phoen], a compatriot of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Hamad, about the first order from the Bahraini prince. Do you remember the name of the prince who gave you that order?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: The name of the prince is Hamad Al-Khalifa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hamad, did that prince have any pseudonym or any nickname that he went by during the time of the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes. He was known as Abu Fatih or Abu Muhammed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, approximately what month or year the Bahraini prince ordered you to go to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but I know that this was after August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hamad, what happened to this Bahraini prince?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: He was killed here during the war at Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you received the order from the Bahraini prince to go to Bosnia, did you in fact, sir, go to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: No, because I was not in the mood for waging war. The war in Afghanistan affected me seriously. So I tried to find excuses. But in the end Prince Hamad understood me and said they could overcome this hesitation on mine but that I should come later. And this happened three months after my conversation with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask for assistance from the technical booth. We would like to show it this witness a video clip, which is from PT06111, at time code 28 minutes 47 seconds. The English transcript of that tape begins on line 1 of page 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the technical booth please give us assistance as requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: "During the September of 1992, the first Mujahedin offensive operation against the Serb was carried out under the leadership of the Bahraini Prince Muhammad Al-Fatih Al Bahraini, with Sheik Anwar Sha'baan as second in command. "The Bosnian Muslim forces had been informed, and Allah willed for them to join the Mujahedin. A group of them participated in the operation. The Mujahedin moved toward the Serb front line penetrating and gaining control over these areas, inflicting heavy defeats on the enemy of Allah. At this time the Bosnians did not have a complete understanding of Islam, [indiscernible] al-Qaeda, and understanding of why they were fighting. In addition to this, their limited military capabilities on the front line meant that they were unable to hold their positions due to the heavy Serbian shelling. "Muhammed El-Fatih El-Bahraini came from Bahrain to the land of jihad in Bosnia after he had abandoned the world with all its attractions. He was a prince of the royal family in Bahrain. He was married. However, the responsibilities of married life did not prevent him from going to jihad. His wife would encourage him to go for jihad. He was also convinced of the need to go to the land of Bosnia by a dream in which he was being called to jihad in the mountains of the Balkans. At this time, he did not know what the Balkans were. Once his dream had been interpreted and he was informed that the Balkan mountains were in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he answered the call to jihad and made his way to the Balkans. Muhammad Al-Fatih had participated in the jihad of Afghanistan where he gained a high level of military experience. "Brother Abu Sahar [phoen] from Egypt, who lived with El-Fatih, says of him : '[Foreign language spoken].'"

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, the video clip that we just saw, did that depict the Bahraini prince that you were telling us about earlier this morning?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would ask that this video clip be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The video clip is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 317.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, you also told us that after the Bahraini prince visited you, you were again instructed or ordered to go to Bosnia by Abu Aruf [phoen]. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I'm afraid you made a mistake. When the Prince Hamad ordered me to go to Bosnia I refused, and then we agreed that I would go later, and he left for Bosnia with two others. Three months later, I heard that Abu Fatih had been killed, and one of the two men who had travelled with him returned to Bahrain and ordered me to go to Bosnia. So this happened three months after the prince was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, Mr. Hamad, where you went, how you actually travelled to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: From the airport of Bahrain I travelled to Germany. From Germany to Croatia, to Zagreb to be specific, by plane, and then by bus from Zagreb to Split, and from Split to Bosnia, Travnik, again by bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Hamad, what you did during the period you were in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Before I travelled to Zagreb, that is while I was still in Bahrain, I was given explanations where I would go to, Zagreb, who would receive me and who would assist me, and I was told that I had to report to the mosque in Zagreb. I asked these men in Bahrain, "How will I be able to recognise these people in the mosque?" And they said there was no need for me to recognise them. They would recognise me as they would be informed about my arrival in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Hamad, the name or names of any people that you met in Zagreb at the mosque?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I remember only one of them. He was known as Abu Ejmen. It is a false name. I don't know his real name, but I know that there was a group of Sudanese who were working for a humanitarian organisation called The Third World.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you provided with any travel documents by Ebu Ejmen or Third World?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I didn't receive any documents. We didn't use documents in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I think I spent the night at Ebu Ejmen's. He headed the third world organisation. And the next day he helped me to set off for Split by bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did Ebu Ejmen give you any instructions when you set off on the bus to Split?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I received instructions already in Bahrain. Everything was explained to me, so that he didn't tell me much as to what I should do because I already knew from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see Ebu Ejmen after this time in Zagreb when you met him?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes, amongst us Mujahedin in Bosnia during the war. And there was a high degree of cooperation with Ebu Ejmen. This organisation was assisting the Mujahedin in Bosnia, and particularly they assisted me. When I was unit commander, I received food and even some weapons, and at times also some money.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, sir, about the trip from Split to Bosnia? How did you travel from Split to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I travelled by bus, and I was told that during the trip I shouldn't speak to anyone, and I had to get off the bus when we reached Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any point during that trip from Split to Travnik, sir, did any authorities ask for paperwork or documents or travel documents?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I remember that there were many check-points, and these check-points were manned by military police and HVO soldiers and also Bosniaks. They weren't together at the check-points. The HVO had their own check-points, and the Bosniak army had their own. I was told that I shouldn't say anything if any questions were to be asked of me at these check-points. I could in those days distinguish between check-points held by the HVO and the Bosniaks, because the Bosniaks welcomed me with a smile and with the Islamic greeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, do you recall whether there were any other foreign fighters on the bus from Split to Travnik, or were you the only such person?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Before that I have to tell you this: When I arrived from Bahrain at Frankfurt by -- by plane there were two foreign nationals. I didn't have any contact with the two of them because I was told in Bahrain that until I reached the Muslim forces in Travnik I mustn't communicate with anyone for my own personal safety. When I arrived in Zagreb, at the airport I also saw these two mentioned men. They tried to get in touch with me, but I avoided it except for a brief greeting. They travelled with me by bus from Zagreb to Split, and they were also in the second bus that set off from Split to Travnik. And finally, I learnt that they, too, had arrived to join the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just interrupt. Sir, you mentioned that when you got to the check-points controlled by the Bosnian army you were welcomed with a smile and an Islamic greeting. What happened when you got to HVO check-points?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They would address me in English as a foreigner, and they would ask for my documents, for my passport and ID card, and I would show them my passport, not speaking, and they would put a few questions to me in English which I understand, such as where was I coming from, where was I going to. And I did what I was told, that I mustn't respond to their questions but just to show my passport. And when they say that I wasn't responding to their questions, it meant that I didn't understand. They could see that I had a regular passport, a regular visa in order, and so they let me continue with my trip to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, do you recall the approximate date or at least the month and year that you arrived in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I arrived in Travnik in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And were you met by anyone when you arrived in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes. I was met by a young man who spoke Arabic perfectly. He was a soldier of the Muslim forces in Travnik. And I was told when I was Bahrain that somebody would wait for me from the units of the Muslim forces, at the bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Hamad, the name of the person who met you at the Travnik bus-stop who spoke Arabic?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: He was a younger man, and he introduced himself by name, but I don't remember it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And just so that we're clear, do you recall why this person spoke Arabic fluently?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I was surprised. At first I thought that he was an Arab, and I asked him if he was an Arab, and he replied that he was from Bosnia, but he could speak the local language and the Arab language because his father was from Bosnia and his mother was from Kuwait.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And this person who spoke fluent Arabic, did he take you somewhere?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: He was most probably waiting for me to arrive at the Travnik bus station, and when he saw me he approached me, introduced himself, and he told me that he was a member of the Muslim forces in Travnik, and he asked me if I was looking for the command of the Muslim forces and that he was the person who was waiting for everybody who would come from the outside in order to join that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about the other two men that were on the bus? Did you observe them at the Travnik bus-stop?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: They were standing not too far from me. I paid -- I drew the attention of the young man who spoke Arabic that I was not alone and that probably two other foreigners arrived in order to join the Muslim forces, and he also went up to them and had the same conversation with them that he had with me. He asked them whether they wanted to get in touch with the Muslim forces. They confirmed that, and then the four of us went to the Muslim forces command in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, what did you do upon arrival at the Muslim forces command in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: We talked with the brigadier of the Muslim forces. I know that brigadier. His name was Asim, but I don't know his last name. And it turned out that he was informed about my arrival. He greeted me like a brother, as they say in the name of Allah, as a fighter in his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did this Brigadier Asim ask you for any information?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: He didn't ask me about anything other than my false name, because as the Mujahedin during the war here did not use our real names. We never showed our documents to anyone. We used our nicknames. And Asim and all the leaders B and H army knew about that, that we did not give our documents or state our true names, and they accepted that. So all he did was ask me for my false name. He had a notebook with him where he wrote down the false names of all the fighters, the foreign fighters who were in his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And by what false name were you known during the war, Mr. Hamad?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I had these names. I changed these false names, but at the time I was known as Abu Ubeyda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you just tell the Trial Chamber, if you can remember, where the Muslim forces command post was located in September 1992 when you met with Brigadier Asim?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: It was somewhere in the centre of Travnik, and it was about so minutes away on foot from the bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Upon your arrival in Travnik, Mr. Hamad, were you aware of who was the commander of the Mujahedin at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the Mujahedin in September 1992 when you arrived in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: It was Ebu Abdel Aziz. We used to call him Abdel Aziz or "Red Beard," "Crvena Brada." He was the first chief of the Mujahedin in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And did you know an Ebu Abdel Aziz prior to arriving in Bosnia, or was that the first time you'd ever heard of him?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him from Afghanistan as one of the leaders of al-Qaeda and as one of the important people on whom Osama bin Laden always relied, and I had information when I was in Bahrain that Abdel Aziz would be coming to Bosnia when the war began here. I learned that he did come here and brought some $10 million US with him in order to organise the Mujahedin forces that were supposed to be part of the B and H army, and this is how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, do you recall Brigadier Asim telling you anything about Ebu Abdel Aziz while you were at the Muslim forces headquarters in Travnik in September 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: When I arrived at Travnik, at the Muslim forces command, Brigadier Asim indicated that Mujahedin were in his unit and that he was the person who was receiving the first groups of foreign Mujahedin. He told me that foreign Mujahedin were at two locations. One was in Mehurici where there was a Mujahedin command at the school and where there was a Mujahedin camp. This was in Mehurici. They also had a Mujahedin front at Karaula. Karaula is the name of a group of villages, and we were in Gradina. All of this was explained to me by Brigadier Asim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Upon first arriving in Travnik in September 1992, Mr. Hamad, how long did you remain in that town?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: You mean in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I arrived before dark, and I left for the Karaula front the same evening, because it happened that a truck with Bosniak soldiers was going to Karaula by chance, so then I left with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And just so we're clear then, sir, you only spent a matter of hours in Travnik before leaving for Karaula?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did you do upon arrival in Karaula?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I arrived at Karaula in the night. I didn't see anyone. The soldiers who were in the truck told me, pointing at a house, that the Mujahedin were staying in that house. The next day I met the Mujahedin who were actually billeted in that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll ask you about Karaula in a moment, but I neglected to ask you a couple of other questions about the time you were in Travnik, that very short period of time you were in Travnik. Were you given anything by anyone while you were in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I was given a military uniform and weapons, infantry weapons. This was an order from Brigadier Asim. And then some Bosniak soldiers gave me that or issued that from their military warehouse, and then I left for Karaula.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Hamad, what type of weapons you were issued or given?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but I think that it was a rifle of Yugoslav manufacture, and then I was given several rounds of ammunition and a few hand grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's now return to Karaula. You told us about a house, and did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just interrupt. What uniform were you given on this day when you were given this arms and ammunition? You said you were given a uniform. What uniform was this that you were given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Members of the B and H army had different uniforms at the time. They had Russian-made uniforms, US-made uniforms. Mostly it was the same uniform used by members of the B and H army. It's the multicoloured green coloured uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Were there any insignia on the uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that period the B and H army didn't use insignia, because the B and H army itself was not organised properly. There were some insignia that just was popping up somewhere, but mostly they were not using insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At least at the time you were issued this uniform there were no insignia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm thinking of the uniform that I received. That didn't have any insignia, but other local soldiers, the majority of them did have insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you -- can you describe the insignia that were on the local soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I will not be able to describe that. This happened a long time ago, 14 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis. I'm sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, let's talk now about this house that you mentioned in Karaula. Is that the location where you stayed?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes. The Muslim forces command provided this house for us -- or, rather, they spoke with the owner of the house to let us use the ground floor where we were staying. The family who were the owners of the house lived on the top floor. Actually, I don't remember if we were upstairs or downstairs. I forgot that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And this house was in the hamlet of Gradina, which is included in the larger Karaula area?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long -- how long did your unit remain in this house in Gradina?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but I think it was a few months, because after the fall of Jajce and its environs we had to leave Karaula without putting up resistance and return to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you a few questions about Karaula and then we'll talk about the time when Jajce fell. At the time you arrived at the house in Gradina, who was the commander of the Mujahedin unit that was billeted there?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: It was a Tunisian known as Ebu Sead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many men were in Ebu Sead's unit based in the house in Gradina in the Karaula area?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I remember that there were about 25 of us foreign Mujahedin - 18 Arabs and 7 Turks - but there were Mujahedin in other places in Bosnia too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And what were the combat objectives of your unit at the time you were in the Karaula region?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: We had two objectives. The first one was to attack Gornji Vakuf and to try to liberate it. But the bigger objective was to defend Travnik from the possible attacks by the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say, Mr. Hamad, liberate Gornji Vakuf, let me ask you, liberate Gornji Vakuf from which military force? Who was in Gornji Vakuf at this time?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: The army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, other than the army of the VRS -- or the VRS and your Mujahedin unit, were there any other military forces in the area known as Karaula?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes. There were members of the Croatian Defence Council at the time we cooperated with the HVO -- or, rather, the Bosniaks cooperated with the HVO, and we as foreign Mujahedin had who were a part of the Bosnian units had to respect that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you mean by "the Bosniaks"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm thinking precisely of members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but I could not call them members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina because it was not formed yet at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, at this period, again September 1992, can you tell us the relationship between the Muslim forces in Travnik and the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: They were very good, and in that period Bosnia -- there were a lot of Mujahedin coming to Bosnia, and there were many such members in Travnik, and that unit there was formed of the best members, and it could receive the Mujahedin. And the members of the Bosniak forces were also religious. They paid more attention to the faith, and this is something that suited to the Mujahedin, and that is why they were sent to the Travnik area. So the relations, of course, were very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the Travnik Muslim forces as a unit, how long did that unit last until?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Could you please ask me the question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely. Did the Travnik Muslim forces continue to exist as a unit throughout the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes, they did exist throughout the war, but the unit advanced. In the beginning you could not call it a brigade because there weren't enough people there. In the meantime, they were able to self-organise as a brigade. They had more fighters, both local and foreign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And at the time that they were able to organise into a brigade, do you know if the name changed or what the name of that brigade was?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: They did have a name. It was a number, but I cannot remember it. The brigade did have a number. Maybe it was the 308th. Something like that, but I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us now about the period of several months when your unit was in Karaula what combat operations, if any, your unit was involved in?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Only in that period?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Only -- only -- you told us that you arrived there in September 1992 and remained there for a few months. During that time period, sir, what was your unit doing in terms of combat operations?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Together with the Bosniak soldiers we participated in the war only in relation to Gornji Vakuf. We were attacking only members of the army of Republika Srpska who were protecting Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hamad, again when you say along with the Bosniak forces, what unit or units are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or more specifically the units of the Muslim forces and other units that were located in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, the names of any of the Bosniak commanders of the units that your Mujahedin were fighting alongside with? Again in this period while you were at Karaula after September 1992.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember a few officers who were commanding the Muslim forces. They were company commanders. For example, Ramo Drmic, known as Ebu Jihad. I know of one person called Faik. I don't know his last name, but I know that he was from Kakanj. I know about Juka and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The persons that you told us about that received you in Travnik, Brigadier Asim, did you ever see him after that period when you were at the Muslim forces headquarters in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes. We were in his unit, and I know that he fought in the Travnik area until midway through the war. After that he left Travnik and returned to his home area where he comes from, to Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Earlier this morning you told us that your unit left -- left Karaula after the fall of Jajce. Do you remember, sir, approximately when that was that Jajce fell?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I don't recall that, but we were in Karaula for a short period of time. Perhaps two to three months, I think, if not less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where did the Mujahedin unit that you were a member of go after Jajce fell?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: We went with the Mujahedin forces to the headquarters of the Mujahedin in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Before travelling to Mehurici did you receive any orders from anyone?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: We had contact via radio with our leaders in Mehurici, and they ordered that we continued along the way to Mehurici, because we foreign Mujahedin do not take orders from anyone but our own chiefs, which doesn't mean, however, that we were fighting independently. And this does not mean that we were not under the control of the BH army, because there was a certain organisation between the BH leaders and the Mujahedin leaders, and these leaders would agree on what was to be done. And after agreement with the BH army leaders, then our chiefs would issue us orders, being foreign Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, I think we'll get to this subject in more detail later today, but can you tell the Trial Chamber what the basis is for the statement that you just made about the relationship between the foreign Mujahedin and the army of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Because after that I became a commander of a combat unit, and I had contact and talks with senior officers of the BH army. And also as a unit commander, I communicated with Mujahedin leaders in Travnik, so that I knew that this organisation existed. And what is most important, we foreign Mujahedin didn't carry out a single attack without the cooperation of members of the BH forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us, Mr. Hamad, that you received orders to go from Karaula to Mehurici. How long did you remain with your unit in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I think that before we left Mehurici we spent a couple of days in Travnik. We had a house in Travnik. The Bosniak soldiers gave us this for our convenience so that we use it as a place of rest. And after that we travelled to Mehurici, and from Mehurici that same night we went to Bijelo Puce [as interpreted] where our unit was billeted near Travnik. Therefore, as far as I understood it, the Bosniak commanders were in Mehurici also where they met with the Mujahedin commanders after the fall of Jajce, and my understanding was they had agreed where they would house the unit that had left Karaula, among them the Mujahedin. So I gathered that they had already agreed, and they had chosen Bijelo Puce near Travnik. And after this agreement my chief also told me to travel with the Mujahedin to Mehurici, and we were told briefly that we would be accommodated in Bijelo Puce together with other Bosniak units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, when you make reference to your chief, at that point in time who was your chief?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: At that point in time the chief was Ebu Abdel Aziz, as I have said. But also -- but also Fahrudin [as interpreted] El Misri, who was a military expert. And I had more contact with him, and I received orders from him because I was a soldier and he was a military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that there may have been a misinterpretation, because I think what we heard in English was not what you said in Bosnian. This person El Misri, what was his first name or the other name that he went by?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Wahiuddin El Misri. He's from Egypt, and this was his false name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hamad, you again have told us about discussions that took place, you told us, in Mehurici between Bosniak forces and the Mujahedin. When you made that comment, sir, what Bosniak forces were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I was referring to the commanders of Bosniak units situated in Travnik and Mehurici and in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, did you ever observe any leaders of the Bosnian army in the school in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes. That was when I met Mr. Mehmed Alagic. He introduced himself to us as a general for the Travnik area, and he communicated with the Mujahedin leaders in Novo Mijesto where we foreign Mujahedin were billeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about in the camp in Mehurici? Did you ever observe any senior leaders of the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in that camp?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I didn't have occasion to see them in that camp, because I myself did not visit that camp often. But when they came to talk to the Mujahedin, they would meet in the school because the Mujahedin commander was in the school. But they may have been in that camp and I may not know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Hamad, if Ebu Abdel Aziz had contact with senior leaders of the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: As Ebu Abdel Aziz told me himself, he had contact with the military and political leadership in Sarajevo. He told me that he had spoken to Alija Izetbegovic and some senior officers in Sarajevo. He told me that they had given him their full support and that they had agreed with him where he and his unit would be accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know where Mr. Ebu Abdel Aziz is today, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, we're almost to the first recess that we'll take this morning, but before we do that, can you please tell the Trial Chamber who it was that gave you the orders that your unit would be going to Bijelo Bucje?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: The order was given by the newly elected commander -- to the newly elected commander and to me, because I was at the time appointed deputy commander, and it was given to us by Wahiuddin El Misri.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, I know we didn't talk about breaks it at the beginning. I hear you referring to the break. I've been trying to work out how we can work it out to fit in, the fact that we started 30 minutes late. Can I suggest that we go up to 11.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That would be fine. I was aware of a Scheduling Order that indicated we would go until 10.45, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's just been handed to me. So we'll go according to the schedule. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, was it then -- so that I understand what you're saying, Mr. Hamad, was it Wahiuddin who ordered your unit to go to Bijelo Bucje?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And at the same time, he appointed you the deputy commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the unit?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Abu Talha from Egypt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was there anyone else that was appointed to the leadership of your unit other than Abu Talha as the commander and yourself as the deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Allow me to explain this a little. When we set off from Travnik towards Mehurici with another two men, I had a meeting with Wahiuddin El Misri, and he chose the Egyptian Abu Talha for the commander of the unit that would be billeted in Bijelo Bucje near Travnik, and he chose me as deputy commander and responsible for military issues, and he chose a third person Abu El Haris from Bahrain as an advisor and a second assistant. At the time, he held a lengthy speech and said that they had agreed with the local commanders and Alagic himself that all the units in Karaula would be billeted in Bijelo Bucje, and he ordered us to cooperate with the domestic army and that without them we were not allowed to carry out any attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, this will be my last question before the break. You mentioned this third person, Abu El Haris El Bahreyni. We've heard evidence about a Dr. Haris. Is that one and the same person or are they two different people?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: No, it is -- it is not the same person. There's another doctor, Muharis [phoen], from Libya. He was one of the leaders. This is Abu Haris, who is a compatriot of mine. And I said that the prince had reached Bosnia before me with two other men, and one of those two others was Abu Haris.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: All right. I simply wanted to stress that when we're talking about Abu Haris, that's not Dr. Abu Haris who later was a senior commander of the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This would be an appropriate time for the first recess, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a recess and come back at 10.00 -- 11.15. Court recessed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, right before the break we were speaking about the unit that you had been appointed to the position of deputy commander of. Can you tell the Trial Chamber how many men were in your unit?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: In my unit there were 107 fighters, 70 Arabs, about 25 Turks, and maybe about 12 Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you've told us that you were sent or ordered to go to Bijelo Bucje. Where was your unit billeted in that village?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Our unit was billeted in two and later in three private houses in the same village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, were there any other military units in that village?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes, there were several units. Not only from the Muslim forces, but there were other brigades like, for instance, the 312th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long was your unit in Bijelo Bucje?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I think until the beginning of 1993. About four months in Bijelo Bucje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber what your unit was doing during the time period you were in Bijelo Bucje?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Together with the Bosniak units we took part in attacks against the positions of the army of Republika Srpska and the HVO towards Travnik and Novi Travnik, and also we would sometimes travel further afield. At Ilijas we took part in the war, and sometimes men went as far as Igman and Vlasic. So we were active in the area where we were situated, but when necessary we went further away in order to assist the Bosniak units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: As the deputy commander of that unit, sir, can you tell the Trial Chamber how combat operations were planned and organised?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: First the senior officers of BH army would meet with the Mujahedin command in Mehurici. After that, I would receive orders from the Mujahedin command that I need to collaborate with the Bosniak units and to take part in the attacks which they had proposed -- or, rather, the locations that they had proposed, and then the Bosniak officers would come to see me to agree with me as to what we should do. But I always abided by what I was told by Wahiuddin El Misri. For instance, they would come to see me and say that we need to attack a particular location and that it had already been investigated and that everything was ready for the attack, but I refused to do that until I myself do not reconnoiter area. And that's how it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What contact -- let me -- let me ask you this, sir: How long did you remain the deputy commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: This was after the attack on Ilijas in 1992 when the commander of the unit, Abdul Aha [as interpreted] was killed. I was wounded. I spent a short time at the hospital in Visoko and then in Zenica, and then I became the unit commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And for how long, sir, were you the commander of the Mujahedin unit in Bijelo Bucje?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I think until mid-1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would it be correct then, sir, that for approximately six months you were the commander of that unit in Bijelo Bucje?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During that period in the first half of 1993 when you were the commander of the Mujahedin in Bijelo Bucje, did you have any interaction with leaders of the army of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: In that period in that area I had interaction with Mehmed Alagic. This was necessary because, after all, he was a senior officer, and he introduced himself as a general, and I was a unit commander within his corps, so that I always had to communicate with him, to explain to him some of the attacks we had carried out, what had happened, how many we had dead among us and among the Bosniak troops. And I also contacted the unit commanders. Like, for instance, Dervisevic Vahid. I would like to mention that he was not a commander of the Muslim forces in Travnik but a senior officer in the 17th Krajina Brigade with whom I cooperated most in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, in the first six months of 1993 what position General Alagic was holding?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I don't know. I remember Mehmed Alagic as a general of the 7th Corps, and he introduced himself as a general, but it is possible that he wasn't a general when we met him for the first time. But I can only tell you what he told me, and that is that he was a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How -- roughly how many occasions did you meet with General Alagic in the first six months of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly how many times this happened, but I can just say that it happened several times. Sometimes he visited us in Bijelo Bucje on the eve of the attack when we were planning an attack on one of the positions of the VRS or the HVO. Sometimes I would meet with him in Travnik, and sometimes I would have a meeting with him during the attack. When we take over positions from the VRS or the HVO, then he would come to talk to me and to learn from me what had been done and how much progress we had made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, earlier today he mentioned operations conducted by your unit in the area of Ilijas. Do you recall approximately when that combat operation took place?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but I know it was towards the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also told us, sir, about a time when your unit commander, Abu Talha, was killed and you yourself were wounded. Which combat operation was that?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The combat operations that you were engaged in, that you were involved in at the time Abu Talha was killed and you yourself were wounded, when and where was that combat operation?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: If you mean whether the operation had a name, I don't know, but I know that it was in the area of Ilijas. The aim was to open the road to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- can you tell us, sir, what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I was in Bijelo Bucje. Late at night we were sleeping in our house, and I know that a courier arrived from Mehurici by truck, and he passed on a message from Abu Talha, who was the unit commander in Bijelo Bucje, that it was urgent, to choose 27 capable fighters and to go towards Mehurici. At that time, we didn't know what it was about except that we had to go to Visoko to take part in the attack on Ilijas, to deblock the road to Sarajevo. When we reached Mehurici, we met with the -- the expert for military issues, Wahiuddin El Misri, and he addressed me and Abu Talha and mentioned Abu Haris from Bahrain, saying that we need to help the BH army in deblocking the road to Sarajevo. That is, he told us that the BH army had organised an attack on Ilijas to open the road to Sarajevo and that they wanted us also to take part in that attack. I was surprised, and I asked what 27 soldiers could do, and we were told that we just had to give them moral support. And they explained that the BH army commanders said that if these 27 Mujahedin were to be in the front line they would be -- they would give morale to the Bosniak soldiers and that one man would be worth 1.000. And I know that there were another 400 Bosniak soldiers from the Muslim forces, but there were also other units who were billeted in Travnik. When we reached Mehurici, I saw several buses parked in front of the school where the Mujahedin headquarters were situated, and I saw that quite a number of soldiers had come from Zenica, from the 7th Muslim. And the people billeted in Mehurici, they started out with us towards Visoko. Then in Visoko we were joined by several units who were billeted in Visoko and together we attacked Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber how this attack unfolded, what your unit did?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: There was a misunderstanding among the Bosniak units themselves. Even we foreign Mujahedin were not satisfied, but we didn't express our dissatisfaction. The BH army commanders had lied to us when they said that they had done reconnaissance in the area and the action had been properly planned. But when we were confronted with the VRS, we learnt that the area had not been reconnoitred, that the minefield had not been cleared, but nevertheless we had to take part because that is why we were there, to give them moral support. So we Mujahedin were in the front line facing the VRS. Then we entered about 300 metres inside, whereas the 400 soldiers who had come from Travnik took up the lines that we had broken through, and they started setting fire to the trenches and the dugouts. After that I was wounded. About an hour after the beginning of the attack I was taken back to Vusoko -- Visoko. The other Mujahedin and the domestic forces continued fighting until the night. But I was told in detail as to everything that happened until the end of the operation, and I heard this both from foreign Mujahedin and from the local soldiers who took part in this combat operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Hamad, when you say the local Bosniak forces that took part in the operation, what unit or units are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the units of the B and H army. Specifically I cannot tell you which units took part. There was several units that I know about, and there was several units that I don't know. I know, for example, that the Muslim forces from Travnik took part, and the Mujahedin also participated, the 7th Muslim Brigade from Travnik. I know that also a part of the 317th Krajina Brigade participated in the attack, and I know that also the so-called Turkish guerrillas took part in the action. They did not participate in the attack as a separate unit, but they were actually part of the 7th Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now -- excuse me. You just mentioned the Turkish guerrilla, and I would ask you if you could explain to us what this Turkish guerrilla unit was.

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I can confirm that these were criminals who came from Asia in order to take advantage of the war situation and to make money. They came here, and they said that they were Mujahedin and that they were here to help the attacked Bosnian people, but actually that was not the true intention. It was only to make money at the expense of the Bosniak state and the Bosniak people. They were able to do it, however, because the B and H army received us, and it was sufficient to say that we were Mujahedin and that we were here to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said that these Turkish guerrillas were criminals from Arab countries. They didn't come from Turkey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said from Asia. And we know that Turkey is in Asia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us in response to my question about units taking part in the operation from Visoko that the Turkish guerrilla were involved; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And which unit or units were the Turkish guerrilla fighting with?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: They were part of the 7th Muslim from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, other than this occasion in Visoko, were you personally aware of any other time when the Turkish guerrilla were involved in combat?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I don't know specifically, but I know that they participated in several attacks in Zenica against the HVO, and they even confiscated a Praga on a truck from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And for the Trial Chamber's benefit, Mr. Hamad, can you tell us what a Praga is?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: A Praga is a type of weapon, anti-aircraft weapon. So it can bring down from land anything that is airborne. When I say Praga, there are several calibres. When I talk about one, I speak about one that has a range of up to 8 kilometres in the air and 15 kilometres on the surface if the targets are on land. So it is intended not only for destroying aircraft, but it can also be used to destroy everything that is on the surface. For example, a vehicle. It can also destroy a building, and you can even fire at a man from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Hamad, where the Turkish guerrilla were billeted or headquartered or located?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: The Turkish guerrilla was accommodated in a music school in the centre of Zenica where the military police of Sakib Mahmuljin was also located -- or, rather, the military police of the 3rd Corps under the command of Sakib Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the Prosecutor establish the time frame that the witness is speaking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, do you know -- you've told us that the Turkish guerrilla were in the Zenica music school. Do you know when they were located there?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: This is very hard for me to determine time periods. Again, I'm talking about things that happened 12, 13, 14 years ago. But more or less it was in the period from 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many men were in this Turkish guerrilla group?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I would call them small groups, because it was perhaps 10 people from Turkey. But among the foreigners there were also local people, because the foreigners would not be able to act by themselves in Bosnia. They couldn't smuggle cigarettes by themselves if there were no local people to direct them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's return then, sir, to the subject of the combat in Visoko on the day that you were wounded and Abu Talha was killed. Do you recall the names of any of the local military commanders who were in Visoko and Ilijas on that day?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I know Ramo Durmis. He was in the Muslim forces. Also he was a company commander. As for others, I cannot remember. I know a few other names, but -- or I did know a few other names, but I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also told us, Mr. Hamad, that it was your position that the Bosnian army had lied to the Mujahedin about the preparation of the terrain and the reconnaissance of the terrain. As a result of that was there any change in the relationship between the Mujahedin and units of the ARBiH?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: There was always a relationship before that, after that as well, but we just felt that it was not quite honest of them. But we understood them. They lied for just one reason, because they knew when -- if they were to tell us they didn't have a concrete plan, they knew that we would then not participate in the attack. I would be the first person against something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, Mr. Hamad, if that had an influence on decisions you took concerning the unit under your command with respect to planning and operations?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase the question? I didn't quite understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: As a result of this operation where you told us that the Bosnian army had lied to you, did that have an influence on your decision-making in the future concerning the planning of military operations?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes. The consequence was that we were very strict towards the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We didn't have much confidence in what they said. So our procedure was such that they would propose a location to us where we were supposed to attack. We would accept that. But regardless of them surveying the terrain and regardless of them having their plan, we would then put very strict conditions to them. If they respected these conditions we would participate in the attack. If they did not respect them we wouldn't participate in the attack. For example, the conditions were that they had to give us enough time for us ourselves to carry out reconnaissance of the terrain, and to give us a few men who were from that area who knew the terrain well so that we would use them when we embarked on the attack. Often we also requested that the attack be under our control -- or, rather, we would participate in the attack, but we would decide when the attack would begin and when would it finish. And they would always accept our conditions, so that we fought within the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the beginning until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, I want to clarify part of what you just said to us, if possible. You said that the Bosnian army always accepted your conditions. Is it your testimony, sir, that the Mujahedin never refused to engage in combat operations with the ARBiH?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: When I was the unit commander, I never refused any attack. And where our command in Mehurici was, on their part they had activities with the ARBiH, but I don't know if they refused or not. In any case, I never refused any attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's explore the flip side of that situation. You told us earlier that Wahiuddin had ordered you not to engage in combat without clear orders. Did your unit ever do that? Did you ever go into combat on your own without specific orders from a higher authority?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: No. We were very strict about that. Wahiuddin gave me permission to participate in the attack in the area where I was with my unit without asking him first but on condition that I had to cooperate with the B and H army. We could not attack any location without asking them, but I myself also had to organise the reconnaissance of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At this point in time, sir, that is the first six months of 1993, do you know approximately how many foreign Mujahedin were in the area near Travnik and Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: When I arrived in Bosnia in 1992 in September, there weren't many of us. There were very few of us. For example, at Karaula there were 25 of us Mujahedin. In Mehurici, in the camp as well as at the command, there were about 15 Mujahedin. The number mentioned was under the command of the Muslim forces, but there were also some other Mujahedin groups which were not in the Muslim forces -- or, rather, they were then not under the control of Abdul, Abu Aziz, such as a group that was in Tesanj. There were about 10 Mujahedin there. In Zeljezni there were about 12 Mujahedin, and about 14 Mujahedin in Konjic, and another small group that was in Bistricak. I can say that -- or, rather, when I arrived in Bosnia I found about 75 foreign Mujahedin more or less already here. After that, probably quite fast, the number of foreign Mujahedin present began to grow, because at some point there were from 300 to 1.500 foreign Mujahedin present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, let me focus your attention on the period around June 1993. Towards the end of the period you were the commander of the unit in Bijelo Bucje. Approximately how many foreign Mujahedin were in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Central Bosnia June 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I think there were about 500 Mujahedin in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the assistance of the audiovisual booth I would like to show the witness another video clip. This also comes from PT06111. The time code is 44 minutes, 2 seconds, until 55 minutes, 14 seconds. And on the English transcript it runs from line 12 of page 17 through line 23 of page 21. If that could please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the technician booth please help us with the video clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: "On the 29th of December, 1992, the second Visoko operation was carried out under the command of the Egyptian Abu Talha. The Mujahedin moved from the front line of Bijelo Bucje near Travnik to the mountains. These are the mountains that overlook the city of Ilijas, which is five kilometres away from Sarajevo. The mountains were liberated, and the Mujahedin continued advancing until they reached some difficult territory. There was then an aerial attack carried out by the Serbs with the use of helicopters. The fighting continued from the morning until the time of the [indiscernible]. The enemy were defeated. Vast areas were liberated, and the city of Ilijas nearly fell into the hands of the Mujahedin. The Bosnian forces were not able to maintain the positions gained, and the Arab brothers found themselves deserted in vast areas, so they were forced to withdraw. A large number of the brothers were injured, and seven the foreign Mujahedin were killed. [Foreign language spoken]."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: "He was a student of knowledge who graduated from the Islamic university of Medine [phoen]. He preferred martyrdom in Allah's sake to the certificate of this world and its false position. He left his studies to carry out jihad in the land of the Balkans to implement what he had learned. He was the commander of the Arabs in the second Visoko operation, due to his good manners and character, his good dealings with the brothers and his knowledge of Sharia. One of the brothers recalls the events surround being Abu Talha's death. "[Foreign language spoken]. "Abu Mahmood of Palestine personified the saying of the hope: 'I will sacrifice my soul. I will throw myself towards death. There is either the noble life which pleases others or a death which puts fear into the enemy.' Abu Mahmood of Palestine was studying medicine at a university in France. Then Allah willed for him to become a practising Muslim. So he left France with his French friend Ebu Aleed [phoen] in order to wage jihad in Bosnia. After two months of his stay in Bosnia, he decided to return to France. He stayed in Zenica for two days awaiting the time of departure, but Allah had chosen a different journey for him to the ever-lasting paradise of palaces and beautiful maidens. "The Algerian brother Abu Muhaijir tells us how Abu Mahmood was killed: [Foreign language spoken]. "After the one has tasted the sweetness of jihad, he cannot take pleasure in the worldly life. There we have Abu Maryam al Afghani who lived in Germany with his German wife calling people to Islam. He led a good life with all its comforts, but there is a difference between the one who has divorced the worldly life and the one who has embraced it. Abu Maryam al Afghani had previously participated in the Afghan jihad, and in Germany he was extensively involved in [indiscernible] programmes calling people to Allah. When Abu Maryam decided to return to jihad, his parents stood in the way. So his wife spoke to her parents, convincing them about the importance of his going to jihad in Bosnia. This reminds us of some of the wives of the noble companions of the Prophets of Allah who encourage their husbands to go to the jihad. So Abu Maryam travels to Bosnia together with his best friend and companion Abu Hudaifah al Afghani, who was also his work colleague. [Indiscernible] bestowed the two of them with acts in his obedience, recitation of the Koran, beautiful characters, and eagerness in the series of their fellow Mujahedin. "Abu Maryam used to clean the toilets and wash the dishes in times of extreme cold. The guarding of the front lines was his preparation for the second Visoko operation. And so Abu Hudaifah asked the permission of his commander to participate in this operation with Abu Maryam, and in the beginning of the operation Abu Maryam was killed. It was only a few moments later that his brother Abu Hudaifah joined him. "How many are the people that seek fame and wealth today? And what of someone who has left all of that in pursuit of Allah's pleasure? Abul-Harith was a famous football player in Bahrain. A lot of the youth today yearn to attain his level of fame. He left his football career behind him and went to Afghanistan to take part in the jihad, seeking to die in the path of Allah. He then went to participate in the jihad in Bosnia. He had devoted his past and his soul to the worship of Allah, and he sets a good example with his manners and manhood. He was always seen reading the Koran, serving his brothers, and guarding the front line. He was characterised by a smile that never left his face and a level of patience such that he never became angry at his brothers. He personified the saying of the Prophets of Allah, 'A smile to your brother is a form of charity.' "A few days before the operation Abul-Harith was seen to take great care of himself, and he wore his best clothes as if he knew he had an appointment with the beautiful women of paradise. "When the battle had reached its most intense stage and the souls of the martyrs had been raised, Abul-Harith found Abu Maryam's spread on the ground, his soul having been raised. He kissed him and said, 'O Allah, join us with him.' He advanced towards the enemy from an area providing little cover, and whilst he was falling on the ground he was hit by a sniper bullet and he surrendered his soul to Allah. "The land of the Ottomans was not left out of sending volunteers of its youth to participate in jihad for Allah's sake. This response from the church is to be expected, since Turkey was the capital of the last Islamic Palace. "Imraan from Turkey went to Bosnia to fight the enemies of Allah. He was 17 years old, of Turkish origin, and was living in America. He undertook the necessary military training, and after two months he had the intention to return to America with a young orphan child who he wanted to adopt. He stayed with his Palestinian brother Abu Muhammed [phoen] in Zenica awaiting his time of departure. When news of the high alert situation reached him, he preferred to stay than to travel, and he answered the call so that he could meet his Lord and be free from the suffering and pressures of this world and to be free from living amongst the disbelievers in America."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hamad, this video clip that you've just been watching, does that relate to the second Visoko operation you've testified about here today?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The individuals that we saw profiled on this video clip, did you -- did you know those people?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: I knew five of the foreign Mujahedin killed. I didn't know the other two, the Turks. Five were killed from my unit. I don't know the two Turks, because most probably they participated in the battle among the Turkish guerrilla in the 7th Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And of the five people in your unit that were killed on that day, do you recall the names of those people?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us the five that we saw on that film that were in your unit?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Unit commander Egyptian -- Egyptian Abu Talha, advisor and second deputy of the unit from Bahrain. Ebu El Haris. A new soldier in my unit who was there for a very short time, Ebu Mahmud El Misri. Abu Maryam from Afghanistan, and Ebu Hudeyfa [phoen] from Afghanistan who had come to Bosnia from Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that this video clip be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The video clip is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 318.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would now ask that the witness be shown a document. This is Exhibit 121. I believe it was distributed or made available in the PT version, which should be in the binders that were circulated under number 1024. And again for the record, PT01024 has been admitted as Exhibit 121. So what the witness is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you just say those references again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It should be in the binders under the number 1024. But again, it's been admitted as Exhibit 121.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hamad, have you finished reading this document?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Does this document relate to any combat operations that you personally were involved in?

utterances.speaker: ALI AHMAD ALI HAMAD
utterances.text: Yes, it does relate to the Visoko operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
